solution.concept_anchor: Indus basin area — India's share and total basin geography

statement_analysis.statement: The Indus river system's total basin area is approximately 1.16 million square kilometres, of which India's share is nearly half.
statement_analysis.reason: India's share of the Indus basin is approximately 321,289 sq km — roughly 9.8% of India's area and about 27-28% of the total Indus basin, not nearly half. The majority of the basin lies in Pakistan.

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike peninsular Indian rivers which peak in August-September, Indus tributaries tend to reach peak discharge in June-July due to snowmelt dominance before monsoon onset.
statement_analysis.reason: Indus tributaries experience earlier peak flows driven by snowmelt (June) followed by a monsoon boost (July-August). Peninsular rivers peak later, in August-October, driven by post-monsoon rainfall.

statement_analysis.statement: India's share of the Indus drainage basin constitutes approximately 9.8% of the country's total geographical area.
statement_analysis.reason: India's share of the Indus basin (~321,289 sq km) as a proportion of India's total area (~3.29 million sq km) is approximately 9.8% — a standard geographic statistic.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know India is one of the basin countries may estimate a larger share, especially if they confuse 'India's share of the basin' with 'basin's share of India's area.'
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Total Indus basin ~1.16 million sq km; India's share ~321,289 sq km. India's share is ~28% of the total basin, not nearly half. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Earlier peak discharge in June-July for snowmelt-fed Indus tributaries vs. August-October for monsoon-fed peninsular rivers — correct hydrology. Statement 2 IS correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: 321,289/3,287,263 ≈ 9.8% — India's Indus basin share as percentage of India's area. Statement 3 IS correct.
Only Statement 1 is NOT correct — answer is (a): 1 only. Correct_option should be 'a'. Correcting.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 plants 'nearly half' as the trap — exploiting the fact that India is a major Indus basin country and students may not know the precise proportion. The basin is shared among India, Pakistan (largest share), China (Tibet), and Afghanistan. Pakistan holds the majority of the basin. Students who confuse the total basin area with India's relative significance often overestimate India's geographic share.
solution.final_explanation:
The Indus basin's geographic extent and its distribution among riparian countries are important for both physical geography and geopolitics.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: India's share (~321,289 sq km) is approximately 27-28% of the total Indus basin (~1.16 million sq km), not nearly half. Pakistan holds the largest share of the basin. This is the planted incorrect statement.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Snowmelt-dominated flow brings Indus tributaries to peak discharge in June-July. This is earlier than peninsular rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery peak in August-October) and reflects the dual-source character of Himalayan rivers.
• Statement 3 — Correct: India's Indus basin area as a fraction of India's total territorial area is ~9.8% — this means roughly one-tenth of India lies within the Indus drainage.

Value Addition:
• The other riparian countries in the Indus basin are China (Tibet — upper Indus and Sutlej headwaters) and Afghanistan (Kabul River tributary).
• Pakistan's share of the Indus basin is the largest — over 60% of the total basin area.
• India's eastern river allocation under IWT (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) represents only the eastern fringe of the Indus basin.

solution.concept_anchor: Zaskar River joins Indus at Nimmu — Chadar Trek frozen river
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because the Shyok is also a left-bank tributary and a well-known Ladakh river — students may choose it over Zaskar for the confluence at Nimmu.
elimination_logic: The Chadar Trek is conducted on the frozen surface of the Zaskar River in winter — this anchors Zaskar as the river famous for being frozen.
The Zaskar River joins the Indus at Nimmu — a documented geographic fact.
Eliminate (a) Nubra: Nubra joins Shyok, not Indus directly, and the Chadar Trek is not on Nubra.

Eliminate (c) Shyok: Shyok joins the Indus but the Chadar Trek is not on Shyok. Eliminate (d) Hanle: Hanle is a river in southeast Ladakh draining toward the Indus but is not associated with the Chadar Trek. Confirm (b) Zaskar.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Shyok River is the geographic-swap distractor — it is also a left-bank Indus tributary in Ladakh and is arguably more discussed in strategic geography (Siachen connection). Students who associate 'left-bank Ladakh tributary' with Shyok may choose option (c). The Chadar Trek is the unique cultural-geographic identifier for the Zaskar — recognising this qualifier leads directly to the correct answer.
solution.final_explanation:
The Zaskar River is one of the most geographically and culturally distinctive rivers in the Indus system — its extreme winter conditions make it a frozen highway.

• Option (a) — Nubra: Incorrect. Nubra joins the Shyok River, not the Indus directly. The Chadar Trek is not on the Nubra.
• Option (b) — Zaskar: Correct. The Zaskar River is a left-bank tributary of the Indus, joining it at Nimmu near Leh. In winter, when the river freezes solid, it forms the 'Chadar' (sheet of ice) that serves as a trekking highway connecting remote Zanskar valley villages to Leh — a famous adventure tourism and cultural geography feature.
• Option (c) — Shyok: Incorrect. Shyok is also a major left-bank Indus tributary in Ladakh but joins the Indus further northwest. The Chadar Trek is not associated with Shyok.
• Option (d) — Hanle: Incorrect. The Hanle River drains the southeastern Changthang plateau into the Indus but is not associated with the Chadar Trek.

Value Addition:
• 'Zaskar' and 'Zanskar' are used interchangeably — the Zanskar region of Ladakh is named after this river.
• The Chadar Trek is typically conducted in January-February when the river freezes 50-60 cm thick.
• The Zaskar Range lies between the Zaskar River and the Great Himalayas — it is the range that separates the Indus from Ganga drainage.

solution.concept_anchor: 2014 Kashmir floods — Jhelum, western disturbances plus monsoon interaction
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know both the 2014 Kashmir floods and western disturbances are true facts may assume the causal link between them is also correct without scrutinising whether western disturbances were the proximate cause of the September 2014 floods.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? The 2014 Kashmir floods were caused by Jhelum overflowing after exceptionally heavy rainfall — A is factually correct.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? Western disturbances do bring winter precipitation to the upper Indus catchment — R as a general statement is correct.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? The 2014 Kashmir floods occurred in September 2014 — this is monsoon season, not western disturbance season. The 2014 floods were caused by an unusually active monsoon trough combined with reduced floodplain carrying capacity, not by western disturbances. R does not explain A.
Both A and R are correct but R does NOT causally explain A — correct option is (b). Correcting correct_option to 'b'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a temporal causation trap. Western disturbances are a real feature of the Indus catchment's hydrology (October–March), but the 2014 Kashmir floods occurred in September — during the tail end of the monsoon season, not the western disturbance season. Students who correctly identify both facts as true and then assume any climate cause associated with Indus rivers explains a flood event there will select option (a). The precise seasonal timing distinguishes the valid fact (western disturbances exist) from the invalid causal claim (western disturbances caused the September floods).
solution.final_explanation:
The 2014 Kashmir floods represent one of the worst natural disasters in the region's recent history, and their cause is a testable geography-environment topic.

Assertion (A) analysis: Correct. In September 2014, exceptionally heavy rainfall caused the Jhelum to overflow its banks, inundating large parts of Srinagar and surrounding areas. The floods killed hundreds and caused massive economic damage.

Reason (R) analysis: Correct as a general fact. Western disturbances are extra-tropical cyclones originating in the Mediterranean that bring winter and early spring precipitation (snowfall and rain) to the upper Indus catchment — a genuine and important hydrological feature.

Causal relationship: The 2014 floods occurred in September (monsoon peak), not during western disturbance season (November–March). The proximate cause was an active monsoon trough combined with reduced floodplain absorption capacity due to encroachment of the Jhelum floodplain. Western disturbances were not involved. R is a true fact but does not explain A.

Value Addition:
• Western disturbances contribute to the dual-peak flow regime of Indus rivers — a feature absent in peninsular rivers.
• The 2014 Kashmir floods caused estimated damages exceeding ₹1 lakh crore — a recurring reference in disaster management discussions.
• Wular Lake's reduced water storage capacity (due to siltation and encroachment) diminished its natural flood buffering role during the 2014 event.

solution.concept_anchor: Ghaggar-Hakra paleo-geography and Harappan archaeology

statement_analysis.statement: The Ghaggar-Hakra river system, now a seasonal stream, is considered by many scholars to represent a paleo-channel of the ancient Saraswati river and contains numerous Harappan archaeological sites.
statement_analysis.reason: The Ghaggar-Hakra follows a course between the Indus and Ganga basins through Haryana, Punjab, and Rajasthan. Many Harappan sites (including Rakhigarhi, Kalibangan, and Banawali) are located along its course, and it is widely debated as the course of the Vedic Saraswati.

statement_analysis.statement: Harappa, the type-site that lends an alternate name to the Indus Valley Civilisation, is located on the Ravi River in what is now Pakistan.
statement_analysis.reason: Harappa is situated on the Ravi River in present-day Punjab province, Pakistan. It gives the civilisation its alternative name 'Harappan Civilisation.'

statement_analysis.statement: The political separation caused by the 1947 Partition made an international water agreement necessary because both newly independent nations shared the same river system for irrigation and agriculture.
statement_analysis.reason: The Partition divided the Indus basin between India and Pakistan, splitting river-dependent agricultural infrastructure. Pakistan's canal colonies (fed by Indus tributaries) were suddenly upstream-dependent on Indian territory — necessitating the IWT (1960).

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who know Harappa is in Pakistan may doubt whether 'Ravi River' is precisely correct (confusing it with a nearby river) and eliminate Statement 2, choosing options that exclude it.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Ghaggar-Hakra as paleo-Saraswati with Harappan sites — this is the mainstream academic position supported by archaeological evidence. Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Harappa is on the Ravi River in Pakistan's Punjab — standard archaeological geography. Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: Partition created a cross-border river dependency that necessitated the IWT — historically verified causal explanation. Statement 3 is correct.
All three statements are correct — answer is (d): 1, 2 and 3.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Harappan geography trap in Statement 2 is the key distractor mechanism. Students who confuse Harappa (Ravi) with Mohenjo-daro (Indus) may assume Statement 2 is wrong if they think Harappa is on the Indus. The deliberate construction of three correct statements also tests whether students resist the habit of looking for the 'one wrong statement' and commit to 'all correct' when that is genuinely the answer.
solution.final_explanation:
The archaeology, geography, and political history of the Indus basin are tightly interconnected — this question spans all three dimensions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Ghaggar-Hakra is now a seasonal stream but once supported one of the densest concentrations of Harappan settlements. Sites like Rakhigarhi (Haryana), Kalibangan (Rajasthan), and Banawali lie along its course. Its identification with the Vedic Saraswati remains academically contested but is widely accepted.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Harappa is located on the left bank of the Ravi River in Sahiwal district, Punjab, Pakistan. Its excavation in the 1920s revealed the Indus Valley Civilization — naming rights gave rise to 'Harappan Civilization' as an alternative label.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Radcliffe Line bisected Punjab, placing India's population's Punjabi canal systems (dug during British rule) under threat of disruption when the headworks controlling them fell on the Indian side. This hydraulic partition — more than anything else — drove the negotiation of the IWT.

Value Addition:
• Rakhigarhi (Haryana) is now recognised as the largest Harappan site — larger than Harappa and Mohenjo-daro combined.
• The Standstill Agreement on water sharing broke down in 1948, precipitating the IWT negotiations.
• Ghaggar-Hakra sits between the Indus and Ganga basins — it is an independent, now-defunct drainage system, not a tributary of either.

solution.concept_anchor: Run-of-river hydropower permissible on western rivers — IWT application
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who know the IWT restricts India's use of western rivers may assume any project on a western river violates the treaty, without knowing the specific run-of-river exception.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes India building a hydropower dam on a western river with no live storage reservoir — this is the definition of a run-of-river project.
The IWT explicitly permits India to build run-of-river hydropower on western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) provided no significant live storage is created.
Eliminate (a): India is not restricted from all development on western rivers — only from significant irrigation diversions and live storage. Option (a) overstates the restriction.

Eliminate (c): There is no requirement for Pakistan's advance consent for run-of-river projects within IWT specifications — only for projects exceeding specified design parameters must India notify Pakistan. Eliminate (d): The project is permissible — not a treaty violation. Confirm (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 'scope-extension' trap in option (d) generalises the IWT's western river restrictions to cover all development, when the treaty specifically carves out run-of-river hydropower as a permitted use. Students who recall 'western rivers go to Pakistan' and stop there — without knowing the treaty's nuanced permitted-use provisions — will choose option (d). This is the most policy-relevant distinction in IWT application questions and has direct bearing on the Baglihar, Salal, and Kishanganga disputes.
solution.final_explanation:
The IWT's permitted-use provisions for western rivers are one of the most nuanced — and most tested — aspects of Indus water geography.

Applicable principle: Under Annex D of the IWT, India may construct run-of-river hydropower plants on western rivers provided the project does not create 'live storage' (water stored for later release) beyond specified pondage limits. Diversion for major irrigation is prohibited, but power generation using river flow without significant storage is permitted.

Mapping to scenario: The project described — no live storage, water used for power generation and returned to the river — fits the run-of-river definition precisely. India is exercising a treaty-permitted right.

• Option (a): Overstates the restriction — India is not barred from all western river development. Run-of-river hydropower is specifically permitted.
• Option (b): Correct. The project is permissible under IWT's run-of-river provisions. Pakistan may object to specific design parameters, but the category of project is treaty-consistent.
• Option (c): India does not need prior consent from Pakistan for projects within IWT specifications — notification is required, not consent.
• Option (d): The project is not a treaty violation — it falls squarely within India's permitted uses.

Value Addition:
• Baglihar Dam dispute (2005): Pakistan alleged design violations; World Bank Neutral Expert upheld India's project with minor modifications.
• 'Pondage' under IWT = small daily/weekly storage for power regulation — different from 'live storage' for irrigation.
• The 2023 Indian notice to Pakistan for IWT modification is partly driven by the need to build more storage on western rivers for climate adaptation — something the current treaty framework restricts.

solution.concept_anchor: Ramsar wetlands in Indus system — Dal Lake not a Ramsar site
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because Hokera Wetland is lesser known than Dal Lake, and students may assume the well-known Dal Lake must be the Ramsar site while the obscure Hokera is not.
elimination_logic: The question asks which does NOT share the characteristic of being a Ramsar-designated wetland associated with the Indus system rivers in India.
Wular Lake (Jhelum system, Kashmir) — Ramsar site. Belongs to the group.
Hokera Wetland (Kashmir, Jhelum basin) — Ramsar site. Belongs to the group.
Harike Wetland (Beas-Sutlej confluence, Punjab) — Ramsar site. Belongs to the group.

Dal Lake (Kashmir, connected to Jhelum) — NOT a designated Ramsar site. Dal Lake is ecologically degraded and has not received Ramsar designation despite its cultural prominence. Dal Lake is the ODD ONE OUT. Confirm (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Dal Lake is the most famous Kashmir lake globally — its houseboat culture and tourism prominence make it seem like it must have every environmental designation. In reality, Dal Lake is in serious ecological distress due to pollution and encroachment and has not been designated as a Ramsar site. Wular Lake and Hokera Wetland (both in Kashmir) are Ramsar sites, as is Harike in Punjab. Students who sort by fame rather than by designation will choose Hokera as the odd one out — the exact entity-swap trap.
solution.final_explanation:
Ramsar sites in India's Indus system are a tested geography-environment overlap question, with Dal Lake being the classic trick answer.

• Option (a) — Wular Lake: Correct Ramsar site. Largest natural freshwater lake in India, on the Jhelum system. Designated Ramsar site with significant fisheries and flood-buffering function.
• Option (b) — Hokera Wetland: Correct Ramsar site. A marsh in the Kashmir Valley fed by Jhelum system springs — designated Ramsar site in 2005. Less famous but verified.
• Option (c) — Harike Wetland: Correct Ramsar site. Located at the Beas-Sutlej confluence in Punjab. India's northernmost Ramsar wetland when designated; important waterfowl habitat.
• Option (d) — Dal Lake: ODD ONE OUT. Despite its fame and ecological sensitivity, Dal Lake is NOT a designated Ramsar site. It faces severe degradation from encroachment, weed growth, and sewage inflow. Its exclusion from Ramsar listing is a governance paradox.

Value Addition:
• India has 75+ Ramsar sites as of 2023 — the highest in Asia.
• The term 'Ramsar' comes from the Iranian city where the 1971 Convention on Wetlands was signed.
• Chilika Lake (Odisha) and Keoladeo (Rajasthan) were among India's first Ramsar sites (1981).

solution.concept_anchor: Gobind Sagar on Sutlej; Pong Dam reservoir on Beas

statement_analysis.statement: Gobind Sagar reservoir, one of India's largest reservoirs by water storage capacity, is formed behind the Bhakra Dam on the Sutlej River in Himachal Pradesh.
statement_analysis.reason: Gobind Sagar is the reservoir created by Bhakra Dam across the Sutlej River in Bilaspur district of Himachal Pradesh. It is among India's largest reservoirs and is named after Guru Gobind Singh.

statement_analysis.statement: The Pong Dam (also called Beas Dam), which creates the Maharana Pratap Sagar reservoir, is situated on the Beas River in Himachal Pradesh.
statement_analysis.reason: Pong Dam, officially named Beas Dam, is built across the Beas River in Kangra district, Himachal Pradesh. The reservoir it creates is called Maharana Pratap Sagar and is a designated Ramsar site.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students may confuse Gobind Sagar with the Beas River (due to Beas-Sutlej Link system) and think Statement 1 incorrectly attributes it to the Sutlej.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Bhakra Dam → Sutlej River → Gobind Sagar reservoir. This is a foundational geographic fact in Indian economic geography. Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Pong Dam (Beas Dam) on the Beas River in Kangra district, Himachal Pradesh, creates the Maharana Pratap Sagar reservoir — a Ramsar site. Statement 2 is correct.
Both statements are individually correct — answer is option (a): Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Beas-Sutlej system creates geographical confusion because the Beas-Sutlej Link carries Beas waters into the Bhakra-Nangal system on the Sutlej. Students who know the link exists may assume Gobind Sagar is 'shared' between Beas and Sutlej, or even that it is on the Beas. Similarly, some students confuse Maharana Pratap Sagar (Beas) with Gobind Sagar (Sutlej). Keeping the two dam-reservoir-river chains separate is the testable skill.
solution.final_explanation:
The Bhakra-Nangal system on the Sutlej and the Pong Dam on the Beas are India's two largest dam projects on eastern Indus tributaries — they are often confused with each other.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Bhakra Dam (Himachal Pradesh) on the Sutlej creates Gobind Sagar reservoir. The Bhakra-Nangal project (dam at Bhakra, barrage at Nangal downstream) was called the 'temple of modern India' by Nehru. Gobind Sagar has a live storage capacity of about 7,290 million cubic metres.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Pong Dam (Beas Dam) on the Beas in Kangra district creates Maharana Pratap Sagar — also called Pong Reservoir. It is a designated Ramsar site and an important wintering ground for migratory waterfowl including the bar-headed goose.

Value Addition:
• Beas-Sutlej Link (Pandoh Dam system) diverts Beas waters into the Bhakra reservoir — the two rivers are physically connected by this infrastructure.
• Gobind Sagar is named after the tenth Sikh Guru — it submerged the historic Bilaspur town when filled.
• Maharana Pratap Sagar (Pong reservoir) is India's highest earth-filled dam — Pong Dam at 133 m is higher than Bhakra concrete gravity dam in terms of dam type classification.

solution.concept_anchor: Not all Himalayan rivers are antecedent — scope limitation

statement_analysis.statement: The antecedent nature of the Indus, Sutlej, and Brahmaputra is evidenced by the fact that all three originate north of the main Himalayan range and flow through deep gorges cut across it.
statement_analysis.reason: All three rivers originate on the Tibetan plateau (north of the main Himalayan range), have courses predating the Himalayas, and demonstrate their antecedent character through deep trans-Himalayan gorges.

statement_analysis.statement: All Himalayan rivers, whether originating on the southern Himalayan slopes or the Tibetan plateau, are classified as antecedent in drainage character.
statement_analysis.reason: Only rivers originating north of (i.e., prior to the formation of) the main Himalayan range are antecedent. Rivers like Alaknanda and Bhagirathi originate on the southern slopes and are consequent or subsequent — not antecedent.

statement_analysis.statement: The Indus flows in a north-westward direction through Ladakh — a direction that appears counterintuitive for a river commonly associated with the Indian subcontinent.
statement_analysis.reason: After entering India at Demchok, the Indus flows northwest through Ladakh before turning south near Attock (Pakistan) — not south as most students assume for a 'north Indian' river.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who quickly confirm Statement 1 and Statement 3 as correct may also accept Statement 2 as correct (since all Himalayan rivers are often loosely called 'antecedent' in popular texts).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Indus, Sutlej, and Brahmaputra all originate north of the main Himalayan range and show antecedent gorges — correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: 'All Himalayan rivers' is an over-extension — rivers like Alaknanda, Bhagirathi originate on the southern slopes and are NOT antecedent. Statement 2 is incorrect — eliminate options containing Statement 2.
Evaluate Statement 3: Indus flows northwest in Ladakh — well-documented and counterintuitive. Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct; Statement 2 incorrect — answer is option (c): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits one of the most important UPSC traps in this topic — the scope-extension error. Popular geography textbooks and travel literature frequently describe 'Himalayan rivers' as antecedent without specifying the critical condition (origin north of the main range). Students who have encountered this generalisation will mark Statement 2 as correct, not realising that southern-slope-originating rivers like Bhagirathi are consequent. This is the most precisely targeted UPSC trap in the entire topic.
solution.final_explanation:
The antecedent/consequent distinction is one of the most precisely tested drainage concepts in UPSC geography.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Indus, Sutlej, and Brahmaputra are the three classic antecedent trans-Himalayan rivers. All originate on the Tibetan plateau north of the main Himalayan axis, pre-date the mountains, and demonstrate their antecedent character through extraordinary gorges — Indus at Gilgit (~5,000 m deep), Brahmaputra at Namche Barwa, Sutlej at Shipki La.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: This is the trap. Himalayan rivers originating on the southern slopes (Bhagirathi, Alaknanda, Kali, Tista) are not antecedent. They are consequent rivers flowing in the direction of the initial land slope, or subsequent rivers exploiting weak structural zones. Only trans-plateau rivers qualify as antecedent.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Indus flows northwest through Ladakh — verified cartographically. This is counterintuitive because students associate 'Indian rivers' with southward flow toward the Bay of Bengal or Arabian Sea.

Value Addition:
• Tista (Brahmaputra tributary) and Bhagirathi (Ganga) originate on southern Himalayan slopes — consequent rivers.
• The term 'trans-Himalayan rivers' is sometimes used as a shorthand for antecedent Himalayan rivers — geographically accurate.
• Antecedent rivers are perennial because their headwaters are in glaciated high-altitude zones established before mountain uplift.

solution.concept_anchor: IWT timeline — signing, Baglihar dispute, Kishanganga arbitration, 2023 notice
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who know the Baglihar dispute preceded the Kishanganga arbitration may place the 2023 notice incorrectly relative to the Kishanganga ruling, swapping events (iii) and (iv).
elimination_logic: The IWT was signed in 1960 — earliest event. (i) goes first.
The Baglihar Dam Neutral Expert process concluded in 2007 — second event. (ii) comes after (i).
The Kishanganga arbitration concluded at the Permanent Court of Arbitration in 2013 — third event. (iii) follows (ii).
India issued a notice to Pakistan in 2023 calling for modification of the IWT — most recent event. (iv) is last. Sequence: (i) → (ii) → (iii) → (iv) = option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Baglihar Neutral Expert ruling (2007) and the Kishanganga PCA ruling (2013) are the two most confused IWT milestones. Students who know both events but not their precise years may reverse them, choosing option (c). The 2023 notice to modify the IWT is the most recent development and should anchor the end of the sequence — students who place it before the arbitrations will go wrong on options (a) or (d).
solution.final_explanation:
The Indus Waters Treaty's implementation history involves several milestones spaced across six decades — a chronology question that tests both geographic and current affairs knowledge.

Correct sequence: (i) → (ii) → (iii) → (iv)

• (i) Signing of the Indus Waters Treaty — 1960: Signed in Karachi by Prime Ministers Nehru and Ayub Khan, with World Bank President Eugene Black as witness. The foundational event.
• (ii) World Bank Neutral Expert ruling on Baglihar Dam — 2007: Pakistan had challenged India's Baglihar Dam design on the Chenab. The Neutral Expert largely upheld India's project with minor modifications — the first formal dispute resolution under IWT.
• (iii) Kishanganga arbitration ruling — 2013: The Permanent Court of Arbitration at The Hague ruled on Pakistan's challenge to India's Kishanganga project on a Jhelum tributary. Allowed the project with water-flow restrictions.
• (iv) India's notice for IWT modification — 2023: India formally notified Pakistan to renegotiate the IWT, citing changed circumstances (cross-border terrorism, climate change, population growth). First such notice in the treaty's history.

Value Addition:
• The IWT survived three India-Pakistan wars (1965, 1971, 1999) without being abrogated — testament to its resilience.
• 'Neutral Expert' (World Bank) handles technical disputes; 'Court of Arbitration' handles legal/interpretive disputes under IWT's tiered mechanism.
• Ratle Dam (Chenab) and Pakal Dul (Marusudar) are the most recently contested projects.

solution.concept_anchor: Indus system characteristics — basin, regime, glaciers, sediment

statement_analysis.statement: The Indus river system drains an area of approximately 1.16 million square kilometres, making it one of the largest river basins in Asia.
statement_analysis.reason: The total Indus basin area (~1.16 million sq km) is indeed one of Asia's largest, spanning India, Pakistan, China (Tibet), and Afghanistan.

statement_analysis.statement: The peak discharge of Indus tributaries occurs later in the year (September-October) compared to peninsular rivers, due to glacial regulation of flow.
statement_analysis.reason: Indus tributaries peak earlier (June-August) than peninsular rivers (August-October), not later. Glacial and snowmelt contributions bring forward the peak discharge, not delay it.

statement_analysis.statement: The Indus system carries less suspended sediment load than the Ganga system, despite a comparable total river length, because the upper Indus catchment is largely an arid cold desert.
statement_analysis.reason: Ladakh's cold desert (Trans-Himalayan) catchment generates minimal runoff and erosion, reducing the Indus system's sediment load compared to the Ganga's wetter and more erosive Himalayan and plains catchment.

statement_analysis.statement: Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) represent a distinct and growing hazard in the Indus basin, particularly in the Shyok and Nubra valleys of Ladakh.
statement_analysis.reason: GLOFs are a documented and growing hazard in Ladakh's Shyok and Nubra valleys due to accelerated glacial melt creating unstable proglacial lakes. Historical outburst events from ice dams on the Shyok are well-recorded.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'All four' is a strong distractor because statements 1, 3, and 4 are all correct, and students who do not catch the reversed seasonal timing in statement 2 will select all four as correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Pair 1: Indus basin ~1.16 million sq km — one of Asia's largest. Correct.
Evaluate Pair 2: Indus tributaries peak June-August (earlier), not September-October (later). 'Later' is the trap word — Incorrect.
Evaluate Pair 3: Less sediment than Ganga due to arid upper catchment — correct hydro-geomorphology.
Evaluate Pair 4: GLOFs in Shyok and Nubra — documented hazard. Correct. Three correct pairs (1, 3, 4) → answer is (c) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's 'September-October' and 'later' are the trap words — reversing the actual seasonal comparison. Indus tributaries peak earlier than peninsular rivers because snowmelt adds to their June-July flow before monsoon even begins. A student who reads quickly and only registers 'glacial regulation' as true (which it is) without checking the claimed direction of effect (earlier vs. later) will mark statement 2 as correct. This is a scope-direction trap within a partial-truth structure.
solution.final_explanation:
This question evaluates four distinct characteristics of the Indus system simultaneously — a typical UPSC quantitative-pairing challenge.

• Pair 1 — Correct: The Indus basin's total area (~1.16 million sq km) places it among Asia's largest — comparable to the Yangtze but smaller than the Ob or Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna combined systems.
• Pair 2 — Incorrect: This is the trap. Indus tributaries peak in June-August — earlier than peninsular rivers (which peak August-October). Glacial melt in spring and early monsoon snowmelt bring forward discharge peaks, not push them later.
• Pair 3 — Correct: The arid Ladakh cold desert limits precipitation, runoff, and erosion — producing less sediment than the Ganga's humid, vegetated, and intensively farmed catchment. Despite similar total lengths, sediment loads differ significantly.
• Pair 4 — Correct: GLOFs are a growing climate hazard in Ladakh. The Shyok River's Kumdan ice dam outbursts in the 20th century are historical precedents; ongoing glacier retreat is creating new proglacial lakes at risk.

Value Addition:
• 'Proglacial lake' = a lake formed at the margin of a glacier — the source of GLOFs.
• The Indus basin's arid upper catchment also means less agricultural pressure on water — contrast with the Ganga's highly populated catchment.
• NDMA, ISRO, and DRDO jointly monitor GLOF risks in Ladakh — a governance-geography overlap.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because it correctly links Siachen with Nubra and Rohtang with Beas, but swaps the Shipki La (Sutlej) with Bara Lacha La (Bhaga/Chenab source), where students confuse the two passes.
elimination_logic: Match A (Shipki La): The Sutlej River enters India through Shipki La pass — well-documented designated trade route. A matches 3.

Match B (Rohtang Pass): The Beas and the Bhaga (Chenab source) rivers both trace headwaters near Rohtang — but specifically the Beas Kund is near Rohtang; Rohtang Pass connects Kullu to Lahaul. B matches 2 (Beas headwaters).
Match C (Siachen Glacier): Siachen feeds the Nubra River — the three-step chain to Indus. C matches 4.
Match D (Bara Lacha La): The Bhaga River (which joins Chandra to form Chenab at Tandi) originates near Surya Tal at the base of Bara Lacha La. D matches 1. Correct: A-3, B-2, C-4, D-1 = option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Rohtang Pass and Bara Lacha La are both in Himachal Pradesh and are associated with rivers flowing toward the Indus system. Students confuse which pass is associated with which river: Rohtang is the source area for the Beas (Beas Kund) and also for the Chandra (Chenab source). Bara Lacha La's Surya Tal feeds the Bhaga (the other Chenab source). The Shipki La-Sutlej link is a trade-geography overlap question. Siachen-Nubra is the strategic anchor. All four pairings test different types of knowledge simultaneously.
solution.final_explanation:
This match tests the intersection of passes, glaciers, and river sources in the strategic geography of Himachal Pradesh and Ladakh.

• A (Shipki La) — matches 3: Shipki La on the India-China border in Kinnaur district is where the Sutlej River crosses into India from Tibet. It is also a designated trade route under the Sino-Indian trade agreement. A critical geography-trade overlap.
• B (Rohtang Pass) — matches 2: Rohtang Pass (3,978 m) connects the Kullu Valley to the Lahaul plateau. The Beas Kund (glacial lake) near Rohtang is the Beas River's source. Rohtang also marks the headwaters of the Chandra River (one of the Chenab sources).
• C (Siachen Glacier) — matches 4: Siachen feeds the Nubra River, which flows into the Shyok, which flows into the Indus. The glacier-to-Indus chain is: Siachen → Nubra → Shyok → Indus. Strategic significance: Siachen is the world's highest battlefield.
• D (Bara Lacha La) — matches 1: Bara Lacha La (4,890 m) is the high mountain pass where Surya Tal lake is located. Surya Tal feeds the Bhaga River, which joins the Chandra at Tandi to form the Chenab.

Value Addition:
• Rohtang Tunnel (Atal Tunnel) bypasses Rohtang Pass — strategic all-weather road to Lahaul-Spiti.
• Bara Lacha La is on the Manali-Leh Highway — one of India's highest motorable roads.
• Shipki La trade resumed in 2022 after a gap — geography-current affairs overlap.
